JP-N3-01-001.notes: させられる is the causative-passive: 'be made to do'. する becomes させられる: 練習させられました 'was made to practise'. It implies the speaker didn't want to.
JP-N3-01-001.tip: Causative-passive = made to do, against your will.
JP-N3-01-001.text: 子どものころ、毎日ピアノを{{c1::練習させられました::練習する · was made to}}。
JP-N3-01-001.tr: As a child, I was made to practise the piano every day.
JP-N3-01-001.flag: dup: replaced 子どものとき、母に野菜を食べさせられました (near-identical to N4-08-005); answer 食べさせられました → 練習させられました

JP-N3-01-002.notes: う-verbs usually shorten せられる to される: 飲ませられる → 飲まされる. The person who made you do it takes に: 部長に. Being made to drink by a boss is a classic office complaint.
JP-N3-01-002.tip: Short form: 飲まされる, 書かされる, 待たされる.

JP-N3-01-003.notes: 書く → 書かされる 'be made to write'. The short form is standard in speech. 百回 (a hundred times) shows the burden of the task.

JP-N3-01-004.notes: 待たされる 'be kept waiting': the causative-passive of 待つ. も after 一時間 stresses the length: a whole hour.
JP-N3-01-004.tip: も after a number stresses how much: 一時間も.

JP-N3-01-005.notes: させてもらえませんか asks permission politely: 'could I be allowed to…?'. 帰らせて is the causative て-form of 帰る. It's softer than 帰ってもいいですか.
JP-N3-01-005.tip: Asking permission politely: させてもらえませんか.

JP-N3-01-006.notes: させてください means 'let me': 考えさせてください 'let me think about it'. In business it's also a polite way of postponing an answer.

JP-N3-01-007.notes: させていただきます is a humble way of announcing your own action: 始めさせていただきます 'I'll now begin'. It's heard constantly in speeches and shops; overuse is sometimes mocked.
JP-N3-01-007.tip: させていただきます = humble 'I will'.

JP-N3-01-008.notes: てもらえませんか asks a favour: 'could you…?'. It's politer than てください because it asks whether you can receive the favour.
JP-N3-01-008.tip: Request politeness: てください < てくれませんか < てもらえませんか < ていただけませんか.

JP-N3-01-009.notes: ていただけませんか is the politest common request: 見ていただけませんか 'would you mind looking at…?'. It suits a superior or a stranger.

JP-N3-02-001.notes: に違いない means 'must be, I'm sure': based on evidence (the lights are on) the speaker is convinced. The polite form is に違いありません.
JP-N3-02-001.tip: に違いない = I'm convinced; はず = reasoning says so.

JP-N3-02-002.notes: Nouns take に違いない directly: 犯人に違いありません 'must be the culprit'. It's typical of detective stories and news commentary.

JP-N3-02-003.notes: はずがない means 'there's no way': うそをつくはずがありません. It denies a possibility on the basis of what you know about the person.
JP-N3-02-003.tip: はずがない = it can't be; わけがない is a near-synonym.

JP-N3-02-004.notes: いるはずがありません 'can't be (there)': he's in Tokyo, so he can't be in Osaka. The reasoning is stated in the context.

JP-N3-02-005.notes: とは限らない means 'not necessarily': いいとは限りません. It often pairs with いつも, みんな or 必ずしも to deny a generalisation.
JP-N3-02-005.tip: とは限らない = not necessarily; often with 必ずしも.

JP-N3-02-006.notes: 書けるとは限りません 'can't necessarily write'. The potential form 書ける sits inside: not every Japanese person can write every kanji.

JP-N3-02-007.notes: っぽい means '-ish', often negatively: 子どもっぽい 'childish'. Noun + らしい means a typical example of the noun: 子どもらしい 'just as a child should be'.
JP-N3-02-007.tip: っぽい = -ish (often negative); らしい = typical of.
JP-N3-02-007.register: っぽい casual; らしい neutral

JP-N3-02-008.notes: っぽい after a verb stem means 'tend to': 忘れっぽい 'forgetful'. It conjugates like an い-adjective: 忘れっぽく + なる.

JP-N3-02-009.notes: 安っぽい means 'cheap-looking, tacky', unlike 安い (inexpensive). っぽい turns a fact into an impression. Similarly 子どもっぽい (childish) and 水っぽい (watery).
JP-N3-02-009.tip: 安い = inexpensive; 安っぽい = tacky.

JP-N3-02-010.notes: わけです draws a conclusion: 'that's why, no wonder'. He lived in Japan for ten years, so of course his Japanese is good.
JP-N3-02-010.tip: わけです = no wonder; わけではない = it's not that.
JP-N3-02-010.text: (He lived in Japan for ten years) 日本語が上手な{{c1::わけです::わけです / わけではありません / わけにはいきません / わけがありません?}}。
JP-N3-02-010.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N3-02-011.notes: わけではありません denies part of a statement: 'it's not that I dislike meat'. The reason for the behaviour lies elsewhere.
JP-N3-02-011.text: 肉がきらいな{{c1::わけではありません::わけです / わけではありません / わけにはいきません / わけがありません?}}が、あまり食べません。
JP-N3-02-011.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N3-02-012.notes: わけにはいきません means 'can't', for social or moral reasons: you can't skip an important meeting. The ability is there; duty forbids it.
JP-N3-02-012.tip: わけにはいかない = can't (it wouldn't be right).
JP-N3-02-012.text: 明日は大事な会議があるので、休む{{c1::わけにはいきません::わけです / わけではありません / わけにはいきません / わけがありません?}}。
JP-N3-02-012.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N3-02-013.notes: わけがありません means 'there's no way': he's never studied, so he can't possibly understand. It's close to はずがない but more emphatic.
JP-N3-02-013.text: (He's never studied) 彼にこの問題がわかる{{c1::わけがありません::わけです / わけではありません / わけにはいきません / わけがありません?}}。
JP-N3-02-013.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N3-03-001.notes: うちに means 'while (a state lasts)', implying action before it changes: 若いうちに 'while I'm still young'. い-adjectives go straight before it.
JP-N3-03-001.tip: うちに = while it lasts (before it changes).

JP-N3-03-002.notes: ないうちに means 'before something happens': ふらないうちに 'before it rains'. Literally 'while it hasn't yet rained'.

JP-N3-03-003.notes: うちに can also mean 'in the course of', with a change happening unnoticed: 住んでいるうちに上手になった 'got better as I lived there'.

JP-N3-03-004.notes: あいだ means 'throughout the whole time'; あいだに means 'at some point during'. Being away all summer takes あいだ; cleaning once while mother slept takes あいだに.
JP-N3-03-004.tip: あいだ = all along; あいだに = at some point during.

JP-N3-03-005.notes: とたん after a past form means 'the moment': 立ち上がったとたん. What follows is unexpected; it can't be your own intention.
JP-N3-03-005.tip: とたん = the moment (and something unexpected happened).

JP-N3-03-006.notes: あけたとたん 'the moment I opened it': the cat dashing out was a surprise. に is optional after とたん. The main clause is past, describing what happened.

JP-N3-03-007.notes: 最中に means 'right in the middle of': 会議の最中に. It's usually followed by an interruption. Nouns take の. 最中 is read さいちゅう.
JP-N3-03-007.tip: 最中に = right in the middle of (then an interruption).

JP-N3-03-008.notes: ている + 最中に: 食事をしている最中に 'right in the middle of eating'. The earthquake interrupts the meal. ている is needed with verbs: ×食事する最中.

JP-N3-03-009.notes: ところ shows the stage of an action: dictionary form = about to; ている = in the middle of; past = just done. 今 often comes with it.
JP-N3-03-009.tip: Dictionary + ところ = about to; past + ところ = just did.
JP-N3-03-009.text:
(You haven't left yet) 今から{{c1::出かけるところです::出かける · about to / doing / just did?}}。
(Eating right now) 今、ごはんを{{c2::食べているところです::食べる · about to / doing / just did?}}。
(Got home a moment ago) 今、うちに{{c3::帰ったところです::帰る · about to / doing / just did?}}。
JP-N3-03-009.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N3-03-010.notes: たばかり means 'only recently': 来たばかり 'only just arrived'. Unlike たところ, it can stretch to weeks or months if it feels recent to the speaker.
JP-N3-03-010.tip: たばかり can be weeks ago; たところ is moments ago.

JP-N3-03-011.notes: たばかりなのに 'I only just bought it, and yet…'. ばかり is a noun here, so it takes な before のに. こわれる is the intransitive 'break'.

JP-N3-03-012.notes: たびに after a dictionary form means 'every time': 聞くたびに. It suggests the same feeling or result each time.
JP-N3-03-012.tip: たびに = every time (the same result each time).

JP-N3-03-013.notes: Nouns take の before たびに: 旅行のたびに 'every time I travel'. おみやげ are gifts brought back from a trip. The souvenirs are a social duty for colleagues and family.

JP-N3-03-014.notes: につれて means 'as (one thing changes, so does another)': 年をとるにつれて. Both sides describe gradual change. 年をとる = grow older.
JP-N3-03-014.tip: につれて: both sides change gradually.

JP-N3-03-015.notes: 時間がたつにつれて 'as time went by'. The main clause usually has a change verb: 変わる, なる, 増える. The past tense of the main clause covers both halves.

JP-N3-03-016.notes: ついでに means 'while (you're at it)': 買い物のついでに 'while I was out shopping'. The second task piggybacks on the first.
JP-N3-03-016.tip: ついでに = while you're at it.

JP-N3-03-017.notes: 行くついでに: going to the station anyway, I'll post a letter. 出してきます means 'go and post, and come back'. The past form 行ったついでに means 'having gone anyway'.

JP-N3-03-018.notes: にしたがって means 'as' in the sense of a gradual change, like につれて but slightly more formal: 上に行くにしたがって 'the higher you go'.
JP-N3-03-018.tip: にしたがって also means 'following (instructions)'.

JP-N3-03-019.notes: にしたがって after a noun can mean 'following': 指示にしたがって 'following the instructions'. につれて has no such meaning.

JP-N3-04-001.notes: ても after the て-form means 'even if': ふっても行きます 'I'll go even if it rains'. It's the opposite of たら: the result holds despite the condition.

JP-N3-04-002.notes: たとえ adds emphasis to ても: たとえ高くても 'even if it's expensive'. い-adjectives use くても. Nouns and な-adjectives use でも: 雨でも, ひまでも.

JP-N3-04-003.notes: いくら + ても means 'no matter how much': いくら勉強しても. The result is usually disappointing. いくら here is 'however much', not 'how much money'.
JP-N3-04-003.tip: Question word + ても = no matter what / how.

JP-N3-04-004.notes: 何を言っても 'whatever you say'. Any question word works: だれが来ても, どこへ行っても. The main clause states a result that doesn't change: he won't listen.

JP-N3-04-005.notes: としたら means 'supposing (that)': 当たったとしたら. It stresses that the situation is hypothetical. もし often comes with it.

JP-N3-04-006.notes: 生まれ変わるとしたら 'if you were reborn'. The condition is impossible to check, which suits としたら. 生まれ変わる = be reborn.

JP-N3-04-007.notes: ば…ほど means 'the more…, the more': 練習すればするほど. The same verb appears twice: ば form, then dictionary form.
JP-N3-04-007.tip: ば + same word + ほど = the more…

JP-N3-04-008.notes: 勉強すれば is the ば half of the pattern: 勉強すればするほど. With する-verbs, the second half is just するほど; the noun 勉強 isn't repeated.

JP-N3-04-009.notes: 考えれば考えるほど 'the more I think about it'. The result can be negative: わからなくなる 'the less I understand'. The verb 考える appears in both halves.

JP-N3-04-010.notes: い-adjectives: 安ければ安いほど 'the cheaper the better'. いい at the end is often enough on its own. Nouns use なら: 近ければ近いほど, but 静かなら静かなほど.

JP-N3-04-011.notes: さえ + ば means 'as long as, if only': お金さえあれば. It implies that one thing is all that's needed. The ば form of ある, あれば, completes it.
JP-N3-04-011.tip: Noun + さえ…ば = as long as (that's all it takes).

JP-N3-04-012.notes: With verbs, the pattern is stem + さえすれば: 書きさえすれば 'as long as you just write'. Everything else is taken care of.
JP-N3-04-012.text: この書類に名前を{{c1::書きさえすれば::書く · as long as you just}}、手続きは終わります。
JP-N3-04-012.tr: As long as you write your name on this form, that's all the paperwork done.
JP-N3-04-012.flag: dup: replaced この薬を飲みさえすれば、すぐよくなります (near-identical to N4-03-006); answer 飲みさえすれば → 書きさえすれば

JP-N3-04-013.notes: くせに means 'even though', with open criticism: 知っているくせに 'you know, and yet…'. It's stronger than のに and only used about others.
JP-N3-04-013.tip: くせに criticises others; not used about yourself.

JP-N3-04-014.notes: な-adjectives take な before くせに: 下手なくせに 'despite being bad at it'. 歌いたがる describes his wish from outside.

JP-N3-04-015.notes: わりに means 'considering, for': 値段のわりに 'considering the price'. The result is better or worse than expected.
JP-N3-04-015.tip: わりに = considering; にしては = for (a specific case).

JP-N3-04-016.notes: 年のわりに 'for his age': he looks younger than people that age usually do. Nouns take の. 若く見える = look young: adverb く + 見える.

JP-N3-04-017.notes: にしては means 'for (this case)': 初めてにしては 'for a first attempt'. It compares with a specific standard. The standard is 'a first try', which normally isn't good.

JP-N3-04-018.notes: 日曜日にしては 'for a Sunday': you'd expect crowds. すいている means 'not crowded'. The speaker expected the place to be busy. にしては takes a noun or plain form directly, with no の.

JP-N3-04-019.notes: 場合 means 'in the event of, in case': 雨の場合 'if it rains'. It's formal and common in rules and notices. Nouns take の; verbs go straight before it.
JP-N3-04-019.tip: 場合 is for rules and notices, not one-off plans.

JP-N3-05-001.notes: について marks the topic: 'about'. に対して marks the target of an attitude: 'towards'. にとって marks whose viewpoint a judgement reflects: 'for'.
JP-N3-05-001.tip: について = about; に対して = towards; にとって = for (viewpoint).
JP-N3-05-001.text:
日本の歴史{{c1::について::について / に対して / にとって?}}調べています。
先生は学生{{c2::に対して::について / に対して / にとって?}}とてもきびしいです。
私{{c3::にとって::について / に対して / にとって?}}、家族がいちばん大切です。
JP-N3-05-001.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N3-05-002.notes: によって can mean 'depending on': 国によって 'from country to country'. ちがう (differ) or さまざま often follows. The noun comes straight before によって.

JP-N3-05-003.notes: によって marks the creator in a passive: 作家によって書かれた 'written by an author'. For simple passives, に is used.

JP-N3-05-004.notes: による before a noun means 'caused by': 地震による被害 'damage caused by the earthquake'. It's common in news reports.

JP-N3-05-005.notes: によると means 'according to': ニュースによると. The sentence usually ends with そうだ or らしい to mark hearsay. によれば is a slightly more formal variant.
JP-N3-05-005.tip: によると… is usually followed by そうだ.

JP-N3-05-006.notes: として means 'as, in the role of': 留学生として 'as an international student'. It labels a status or capacity.
JP-N3-05-006.tip: として = as (in the role of).

JP-N3-05-007.notes: 趣味として 'as a hobby'. として can be strengthened with は for contrast: 趣味としては 'as a hobby, at least'. ピアノをひく = play the piano.

JP-N3-05-008.notes: に関して means 'regarding': a more formal について. It's common in meetings, emails and official documents. The noun form is に関する.
JP-N3-05-008.tip: に関して = formal について.

JP-N3-05-009.notes: 新しい計画に関して 'regarding the new plan'. Some speakers use it to sound businesslike even in ordinary talk.

JP-N3-05-010.notes: って is casual for と in quotes: 来られないって 'says he can't come'. The verb (言っていた) is often left out. Rising intonation turns it into a question: 来られないって?

JP-N3-05-011.notes: って can mark a topic someone is asking about: 「すきやき」って何? 'what's sukiyaki?'. It's casual for というのは. The question marker か is dropped in casual speech.

JP-N3-05-012.notes: って as a casual topic marker: 田中さんって、どんな人? 'what's Tanaka like?'. It suggests the speaker has heard of him but doesn't know him.

JP-N3-05-013.notes: において means 'in, at' in formal language, a stiff version of で: 会議室において行われます. It's typical of announcements and documents.

JP-N3-05-014.notes: における is the form before a noun: 日本における外国人 'foreigners in Japan'. において can't go straight before a noun.

JP-N3-05-015.notes: について becomes についての before a noun: 文化についての本 'a book about culture'. The の is needed to link the phrase to the noun.
JP-N3-05-015.tip: Before a noun: についての, に関する, に対する.

JP-N3-05-016.notes: に関して becomes に関する before a noun: 環境問題に関する会議 'a conference on environmental issues'. No の is used here.

JP-N3-05-017.notes: に対して becomes に対する before a noun: お客様に対する態度 'attitude towards customers'. お客様 is the respectful word for customers, used even when talking about them. 態度 = attitude, manner.

JP-N3-05-018.notes: かわりに after a verb can mean 'in exchange for': 教えるかわりに 'in return for teaching'. After a noun + の it means 'instead of': 母のかわりに.
JP-N3-05-018.tip: かわりに = instead of, or in exchange for.

JP-N3-06-001.notes: ほど + negative compares: 去年ほど暑くない 'not as hot as last year'. It only works with a negative; ×去年ほど暑い is wrong.
JP-N3-06-001.tip: ほど + negative = not as … as.

JP-N3-06-002.notes: ほど also shows degree: 死ぬほどつかれた 'so tired I could die'. It's a common exaggeration in speech. The verb before ほど is in the dictionary form.

JP-N3-06-003.notes: 涙が出るほど 'so much that tears came'. くらい can replace ほど in this degree sense. 涙が出る = tears come out. The degree phrase comes before the verb it describes.

JP-N3-06-004.notes: ばかり after a noun means 'nothing but', often critically: ゲームばかり. It suggests the speaker disapproves.
JP-N3-06-004.tip: ばかり = nothing but (often a complaint).

JP-N3-06-005.notes: 文句ばかり言う 'do nothing but complain'. ばかり replaces を: ×文句をばかり. 文句を言う = complain. The ばかり phrase replaces the object particle, and the verb follows directly.

JP-N3-06-006.notes: てばかりいる means 'always doing': 泣いてばかりいます. ばかり goes between the て-form and いる. The tone is critical, even when sympathetic. 毎日 underlines the repetition.

JP-N3-06-007.notes: だらけ means 'covered in, full of' something unpleasant: どろだらけ 'covered in mud'. It's not used for good things.
JP-N3-06-007.tip: だらけ is only for unpleasant things.

JP-N3-06-008.notes: まちがいだらけ 'full of mistakes'. Likewise ほこりだらけ (dusty), 傷だらけ (covered in scratches). 作文 = essay, composition. The opposite idea, full of good things, uses いっぱい instead.

JP-N3-06-009.notes: だけでなく means 'not only': 英語だけでなく、中国語も. The second item usually takes も. ばかりでなく is a slightly more formal synonym. The verb 話せる is the potential of 話す.
JP-N3-06-009.tip: AだけでなくBも = not only A but also B.

JP-N3-06-010.notes: な-adjectives take な before だけでなく: 便利なだけでなく 'not only convenient'. い-adjectives and verbs go straight before it.
JP-N3-06-010.text: この町は便利な{{c1::だけでなく::not only}}、自然も多いです。
JP-N3-06-010.tr: This town isn't just convenient; there's plenty of nature too.
JP-N3-06-010.flag: dup: replaced この店は安いだけでなく、おいしいです (near-identical to N5-08-005)

JP-N3-06-011.notes: こそ singles something out with strong emphasis: 今年こそ 'this year (for sure)'. The implication is that previous attempts failed.
JP-N3-06-011.tip: こそ = this one, for sure.

JP-N3-06-012.notes: からこそ means 'precisely because': 好きだからこそ. It gives a reason that might seem surprising. The sentence often ends with のです, explaining the reason.

JP-N3-06-013.notes: こちらこそ is the set reply to thanks or an apology: 'no, it's me who should thank you'. It mirrors the other person's words.

JP-N3-06-014.notes: さえ means 'even', a surprising minimum: 食べる時間さえない 'not even time to eat'. Everything else is implied to be impossible too.

JP-N3-06-015.notes: でさえ after a noun: 子どもでさえ 'even a child'. It's close to でも but more emphatic and slightly more formal.

JP-N3-06-016.notes: まで means 'even', adding an extreme item to a list: 家族まで 'even my family'. It suggests the list went further than expected.

JP-N3-07-001.notes: ようとする means 'try to', often failing: ねようとしました 'I tried to sleep'. It's an effortful attempt, unlike てみる (try out).
JP-N3-07-001.tip: ようとする = attempt; てみる = try out.

JP-N3-07-002.notes: ようとした can mean 'was about to': 出ようとしたとき 'just as I was about to leave'. Something then interrupts. The とき clause sets the moment of interruption.

JP-N3-07-003.notes: ようとしない means 'won't, refuses to': 食べようとしません. It describes someone else's stubbornness. ようとしない implies the speaker's frustration.

JP-N3-07-004.notes: ことにしている is a rule you set yourself; ことになっている is a rule set by others. Jogging is a personal habit; ties are company policy.
JP-N3-07-004.tip: ことにしている = my rule; ことになっている = the rule.

JP-N3-07-005.notes: べき means 'should, ought to', a moral duty: 守るべきです. する can be するべき or すべき. The negative is べきではない. It sounds preachy towards superiors, so ほうがいい is safer.
JP-N3-07-005.tip: べき is strong; ほうがいい is softer advice.

JP-N3-07-006.notes: べきではない means 'shouldn't': 言うべきではありません. It's a firm moral statement, not friendly advice. 悪口を言う = speak ill of someone.

JP-N3-07-007.notes: ずに means 'without doing', a written version of ないで: 食べずに. The ない form drops ない and adds ずに. The ない form 食べない gives the stem 食べ.

JP-N3-07-008.notes: 言う → 言わずに 'without saying'. Because ずに counts as a negative, 何も can go with it: 何も言わずに 'without saying anything'.

JP-N3-07-009.notes: する becomes せずに: 勉強せずに 'without studying'. ×しずに is a common error. 来る becomes 来ずに (こずに). The meaning is the same as 勉強しないで, but ずに suits writing.
JP-N3-07-009.tip: する → せずに, not ×しずに.

JP-N3-07-010.notes: ないで means 'without doing' (the manner of the next action); なくて gives a reason (something didn't happen, so…).
JP-N3-07-010.tip: ないで = without; なくて = because not.

JP-N3-07-011.notes: ないことはない means 'it's not that I can't': 食べられないことはない. It admits possibility but shows reluctance. The けど clause gives the real feeling.
JP-N3-07-011.tip: ないことはない = it's possible, but…

JP-N3-07-012.notes: 行けないことはありません 'I could go, but…'. The unfinished が… signals reluctance politely. 行ける is the potential of 行く. The unfinished sentence lets the listener infer the problem.

JP-N3-07-013.notes: ことはない after a dictionary form means 'there's no need to': 心配することはありません. It reassures the listener. そんなに means 'so much'.
JP-N3-07-013.tip: Dictionary form + ことはない = no need to.

JP-N3-07-014.notes: わざわざ means 'going to the trouble of': わざわざ来ることはない 'no need to come all this way'. It's a kind refusal of a favour.

JP-N3-08-001.notes: ということです reports formal hearsay: 上がるということです 'I'm told they'll go up'. It's common on the news and in official notices.
JP-N3-08-001.tip: ということです = formal 'I'm told'.

JP-N3-08-002.notes: 来られないということです 'I'm told he can't come'. It passes on a message neutrally, without the speaker's judgement.

JP-N3-08-003.notes: とか at the end means 'I heard something like': vague, half-remembered hearsay. 閉まる (close) is the intransitive of 閉める.
JP-N3-08-003.tip: Sentence-final とか = I heard something about.
JP-N3-08-003.text: あの店、来月閉まる{{c1::とか::I heard something like}}。
JP-N3-08-003.tr: I heard something about that shop closing next month.
JP-N3-08-003.flag: dup: replaced 田中さんは来月結婚するとか (near-identical to N4-07-005)

JP-N3-08-004.notes: 雪がふるとか 'I heard it might snow'. The speaker isn't sure of the source or the details. The tone is casual, as between friends or colleagues. The source isn't given.

JP-N3-08-005.notes: ように言う reports a command: 出すように言いました 'told them to hand it in'. The command itself would be 出してください. ないように言う reports a negative command.
JP-N3-08-005.tip: Reported command: dictionary form + ように言う.

JP-N3-08-006.notes: ように言われました 'was told to': the passive of 言う. 母に marks who did the telling. The passive puts the speaker as subject. The original command would have been 早く帰りなさい.

JP-N3-08-007.notes: ないように注意する means 'warn not to': 飲まないように注意されました 'was warned not to drink'. 注意する also means 'tell off'.

JP-N3-08-008.notes: ますように expresses a wish or prayer: 合格しますように 'may I pass'. It's written on shrine prayer plaques (絵馬).
JP-N3-08-008.tip: ますように = a wish or prayer.

JP-N3-08-009.notes: 早く元気になりますように 'I hope you get well soon', a standard line in get-well cards. The verb is in the ます form even though it's a wish. It's also used for the New Year: いい年になりますように.

JP-N3-09-001.notes: おかげで means 'thanks to' (a good result); せいで means 'because of' (a bad result, with blame). The main clause states the result.
JP-N3-09-001.tip: おかげで = thanks to; せいで = the fault of.

JP-N3-09-002.notes: おかげで after a past form: 薬を飲んだおかげで 'thanks to taking the medicine'. It shows gratitude even towards things.

JP-N3-09-003.notes: せいで blames a cause: 弟のせいで 'because of my brother (it's his fault)'. Nouns take の. しかられる is the passive of しかる (scold). The blame is explicit.
JP-N3-09-003.text: 弟の{{c1::せいで::おかげで or せいで?}}、母にしかられました。
JP-N3-09-003.tr: I got told off by my mother because of my little brother.
JP-N3-09-003.flag: dup: replaced 寝不足のせいで、頭がいたいです (near-identical to N2-02-009)

JP-N3-09-004.notes: ため means 'due to' in formal language: 事故のため 'due to an accident'. It's standard in train announcements.
JP-N3-09-004.tip: ため after a cause = due to; after a goal = in order to.

JP-N3-09-005.notes: 台風のため 'due to the typhoon'. 欠航 means a cancelled flight or sailing; for trains, 運休. The noun 台風 takes の before ため.

JP-N3-09-006.notes: たものだ after a past form means 'used to', with nostalgia: 泳いだものです. よく (often) is common with it. 子どものころ = in my childhood.

JP-N3-09-007.notes: ものだ after a dictionary form states what one should do: 聞くものです 'one should listen'. It sounds like a general rule.

JP-N3-10-001.notes: たまま means 'with (a state left as it is)': くつをはいたまま 'with your shoes on'. In Japan, shoes come off at the entrance.
JP-N3-10-001.tip: たまま = leaving it as it was.

JP-N3-10-002.notes: つけたまま寝てしまいました 'fell asleep with the light on'. てしまう adds regret. 電気をつける = switch on the light. The state continued all night.

JP-N3-10-003.notes: あけたまま 'with the window open'. The state should normally have changed, but didn't. あける is the transitive 'open'. The open window could be a worry: rain or burglars.

JP-N3-10-004.notes: ふりをする means 'pretend': 寝ているふり 'pretend to be asleep'. Verbs keep their plain form before ふり. ふり is a noun meaning 'appearance, pretence'.

JP-N3-10-005.notes: 知らないふりをする 'pretend not to know'. Nouns take の: 学生のふり; な-adjectives take な: 元気なふり. The negative 知らない goes straight before ふり. ふりをする is always deliberate.

JP-N3-10-006.notes: がち after a verb stem means 'tend to (often, and it's not good)': かぜをひきがち. It's only for unwanted tendencies.
JP-N3-10-006.tip: がち = tends to (an unwanted tendency).

JP-N3-10-007.notes: 休みがち 'tends to be absent'. It's a typical phrase in school reports. 授業を休む = miss a class. がち conjugates like a な-adjective: 休みがちな学生.

JP-N3-10-008.notes: がち after a noun: くもりがち 'mostly cloudy'. It's common in weather forecasts. がちの + noun links it: くもりがちの天気. The opposite, mostly sunny, is 晴れがち or simply 晴れの日が多い.

JP-N3-10-009.notes: おきに means 'at intervals of', skipping some: 一日おきに 'every other day'. ごとに means 'each, every one': 駅ごとに.
JP-N3-10-009.tip: 一日おき = every other day; 一日ごと = every day.

JP-N3-10-010.notes: ずつ after a quantity means 'at a time': 少しずつ 'a little at a time'. It shows steady, even distribution.
JP-N3-10-010.tip: ずつ = each, at a time.

JP-N3-10-011.notes: ずつ after a number: 二つずつ 'two each'. 一人 (per person) comes before the number. 取る = take. ずつ means each person gets the same amount.

JP-N3-10-012.notes: のような before a noun means 'like, such as': すしのような日本料理. It gives a typical example. The example is part of a larger group.
JP-N3-10-012.tip: のような + noun; のように + verb or adjective.

JP-N3-10-013.notes: ように after a clause means 'as, in the way that': 先生が言ったように 'as the teacher said'. The past 言った shows the instructions came earlier. Casual: 先生が言ったみたいに.

JP-N3-10-014.notes: なんか is casual for など, 'or something': お茶なんかどう? 'how about some tea or something?'. It softens the offer.

JP-N3-10-015.notes: なんて after a noun dismisses it: 宿題なんて 'stupid homework'. The tone shows contempt or reluctance. やりたくない completes the refusal.

JP-N3-10-016.notes: なんて after a clause expresses surprise: 結婚するなんて 'to think he's getting married'. It's often followed by a reaction such as 知らなかった.

JP-N3-10-017.notes: たて after a verb stem means 'freshly': 焼きたてのパン 'freshly baked bread'. It describes something just made and still at its best.

JP-N3-10-018.notes: できたて 'just made': できる + たて. Restaurants use it to promise freshness. The phrase できたての料理 is often seen on menus. できる here means 'be made, be ready'.
